extracted.intended_audience: general public, students and researchers interested in U.S. Supreme Court labor law cases
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia case summary of the Encino Motorcars v. Navarro Supreme Court litigation concerning overtime eligibility of automotive service advisors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and the applicability of Chevron deference to agency interpretive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference inapplicable to procedurally defective or inadequately explained regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts cannot apply Chevron deference to a regulation that is procedurally defective or lacks an adequate explanation for a deviation from longstanding agency policy; such regulations are arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court held that Chevron deference is only allowable when agencies make regulations with 'good reasons for the new policy'; earlier cases such as FCC v. Fox and Brand X support that agencies must provide adequate rationale for policy changes. If an agency's interpretive rule represents a complete change from prior policy without adequate explanation, a court should not treat that rule as entitled to Chevron deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: FLSA exemption for automotive employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The FLSA exempts from its overtime requirements 'any salesman, partsman, or mechanic primarily engaged in selling or servicing automobiles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central statutory criterion is whether an employee is 'primarily engaged in selling or servicing automobiles.' The parties disputed whether 'service advisors' fit within this exemption. Different courts (Fourth, Fifth Circuits, several district courts, state supreme courts) have interpreted the exemption differently, leading to circuit splits resolved by the Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Labor's 2011 interpretive regulation on service advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2011 Department of Labor interpretive regulation stated that service advisors are not exempt under §213(b)(10)(A) because they do not personally service automobiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretive rule reversed earlier DOL positions (e.g., 1978) and was a key basis for the Ninth Circuit's decision. The Supreme Court found that the 2011 rule lacked adequate explanation for the policy shift, undermining its claim to Chevron deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must provide adequate explanation when changing longstanding policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency reverses a longstanding policy, it must provide an adequate explanation for the change in order for courts to afford deference to the new rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision emphasizes that a mere change of position is insufficient; courts look for reasoned explanation. Absent such explanation, the regulation may be ruled arbitrary and capricious. The Court relied on precedent (e.g., FCC v. Fox) to articulate this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative history may be used to interpret statutory exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ninth Circuit based its rehearing decision primarily on the legislative history of the FLSA when determining whether service advisors fall within the exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates that, in statutory-exemption disputes, courts can and do consult legislative history and other tools of statutory interpretation to determine whether a class of employees is exempt under the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial options when Chevron deference is unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: If Chevron deference does not apply to an agency interpretation, courts must decide whether to resolve the statutory question themselves or remand for agency explanation or reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Thomas (dissent in the first opinion) argued the Court should evaluate the merits and rule on the statutory question rather than merely vacate and remand. The case shows differing judicial approaches to handling the merits once agency deference is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential and practical implications of rehearing the same case
rubrics_metrics.description: The case—heard twice by the Supreme Court—provides insight into how changes in Court composition or timing can affect review of agency rulemaking and statutory interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unusual procedural history (vacatur/remand then rehearing and reversal) highlights how shifts in Court membership and attitudes toward federal rulemaking can influence outcomes; practitioners should note that identical underlying facts may yield different results on re-review.
